claim: Claude Code users and projects cannot override a deny rule defined in managed settings.
why: Managed deny rules let administrators enforce hard limits across user and project settings.
check: For an organization-wide prohibition, check whether the deny rule is in managed settings.
quote: A deny rule defined in managed settings can’t be overridden by any user or project setting.

claim: Claude Code's enterprise guide says subagents inherit the parent session's permission rules, so a broad rule for the parent can also reach its delegates.
why: The enterprise guide describes permission-mode inheritance without exceptions, while subagents-019 documents when explicit subagent modes take effect and when the parent mode overrides them.
check: Check whether broad parent permission rules reach delegates, and verify the effective mode separately when a subagent sets permissionMode.
quote: Subagents inherit the parent session's permission rules and permission mode, so a broad rule written for the top-level session applies to every agent it delegates to.

claim: The enterprise security guide says Claude Code parses Bash commands deterministically and applies deny and ask rules to each part of a compound command in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.
why: Per-part matching lets Claude Code check compound commands, but pattern rules only see the text the agent supplies.
check: Check whether command restrictions are backed by sandboxing and egress allowlisting.
quote: Parsing is deterministic, so the same command gets the same answer every time. Deny and ask rules apply to each part of a command in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.

claim: In Claude Code, a PreToolUse hook can approve some tool calls, but returning allow cannot override a deny rule, an ask rule, or the safeguard on critical-path deletions.
why: The guide puts hook decisions inside the fixed permission boundaries.
check: Flag any PreToolUse allow expected to override a matching deny or ask rule or approve a critical-path deletion on its own.
quote: Hooks sit inside the fixed boundaries rather than above them. A PreToolUse hook can block a tool call, but a hook returning "allow" can’t approve past a deny rule, an ask rule, or a critical-path deletion.

claim: When Claude Code receives managed settings through multiple routes, it uses only the highest-ranked source by default and silently ignores the rest unless managedSourcesBehavior is set to merge.
why: The guide ranks server-managed settings ahead of MDM or OS-level policy and managed files for local sessions, and says only server-managed settings reach Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions.
check: If local managed settings use multiple routes, check the merge setting and use /status on a test machine to confirm which sources applied.
quote: By default, Claude Code applies only the highest-ranked source and ignores the others, in that order, with no warning. If your MDM profile turns on the sandbox and a managed settings file holds the egress allowlist, the allowlist never applies.

claim: The enterprise security guide says the managed allowlist locked with allowManagedDomainsOnly covers shell commands only, so the WebFetch tool needs its own permission rules.
why: The sandbox network list does not govern the WebFetch tool.
check: Check that a locked domain allowlist is paired with WebFetch permission rules, since otherwise web fetches follow different limits than shell commands.
quote: Locked: only your list counts (allowManagedDomainsOnly). The list covers shell commands, so limit the WebFetch tool with its own permission rules

claim: The enterprise security guide says the Claude Code sandbox runs on macOS, Linux and WSL2, not native Windows, so with failIfUnavailable on Claude Code will not start there; it suggests WSL2 or the alpha Windows support in the open source sandbox runtime.
why: Where the sandbox cannot start and failIfUnavailable is off, commands run uncontained instead of being refused.
check: On native Windows machines, check whether a policy that requires the sandbox is set, and whether it was tested there, because strict mode will block startup.
quote: The sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. It isn’t available on native Windows, so with failIfUnavailable on, Claude Code won’t start there. Run it inside WSL2, or try the alpha Windows support in the open source sandbox runtime, which can restrict file and network access.

claim: For sandboxed local Claude Code sessions, Anthropic advises admins to add Read deny rules for credential paths and use credential masking so commands can authenticate without holding the real value.
why: Credentials that the agent can read may leak even when its command execution is sandboxed.
check: Check managed Read deny rules and masking for credential paths, and verify shell-side read restrictions separately.
quote: To combat credential leaks, admins can add Read deny rules for the organization’s credential paths and also set credential masking, which lets a command sign in without ever holding the real value.

claim: The enterprise security guide says Claude Code cloud sessions give each task its own VM in an Anthropic-managed environment, keep GitHub credentials outside it, and suit work that reads untrusted content or runs unattended.
why: They are isolated from the developer's machine and internal networks by default, and VMs can be discarded at any time.
check: For unattended or untrusted-content workflows run locally with broad access, check whether a cloud session or another isolated environment would fit better.
quote: Claude Code cloud sessions run on an Anthropic managed environment with each task getting its own VM. Not only does this contain where Claude can execute, it also keeps GitHub credentials outside the VM.

claim: According to the enterprise security guide, Claude Code cloud sessions are not available to organizations that use zero data retention, the HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.
why: The guide lists this as a limit of the cloud isolation option for regulated organizations.
check: For organizations with zero data retention, HIPAA configuration or customer-managed keys, do not recommend cloud sessions as the containment option.
quote: Keep in mind, cloud sessions aren’t available to organizations that use zero data retention, the HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.

claim: Because Claude Code cloud sessions allow public package registries by default, Anthropic advises setting shared environments' network access to allow only the organization's vetted registry.
why: The egress allowlist is what limits which registries an agent can reach.
check: Check whether public registries remain reachable and consider self-hosted environments (public beta in the guide) when the vetted registry sits on a private network.
quote: Cloud sessions allow public registries by default, so set network access on your shared environments to match, or use self-hosted environments (public beta) if the registry sits on your private network.

claim: The enterprise security guide says owners can publish shared cloud environments developers cannot change, but developers can still create their own, so organizations that need a lock must run sessions on infrastructure they operate.
why: The guide's central-settings table says there is no full lock on Anthropic-hosted environments and no organization-wide allowlist there.
check: If a policy depends on a cloud environment's network or secret settings, check whether developers can bypass it with a personal environment.
quote: Developers can still create new environments and modify those environment settings. Organizations that need to lock this down host their own sessions, running Claude Code on infrastructure they launch and run, so they control the policy for those sessions.

claim: Anthropic's enterprise guide recommends reviewing MCP servers, plugins, skills, subagent definitions, and repository CLAUDE.md files as dependencies.
why: Their descriptions or instructions can reach the agent as soon as they load.
check: Check that each extension or instruction file is reviewed, and look for version pins and marketplace allowlisting where applicable to MCP servers, plugins, and skills.
quote: MCP servers, plugins, skills, subagent definitions, and a repository’s CLAUDE.md file are dependencies too, and they deserve the review you give a package. Unlike a compromised library, which waits to be called, they reach the agent as soon as they load. Their descriptions and instructions enter the context window before the agent has done any work.

claim: Anthropic's enterprise guide advises routing coding agents' DNS through a resolver the organization filters and logs because HTTP allowlists miss DNS exfiltration.
why: HTTP allowlisting alone cannot see data leaving via DNS queries.
check: Where an organization limits agent egress with an HTTP domain allowlist, check whether agent DNS also goes through a filtered, logged resolver.
quote: Route the agent's DNS through a resolver you filter and log.

claim: According to the enterprise security guide, by default an agent in Claude Code runs under the identity of the developer who oversees it, so incident response may need to separate agent actions from developer actions.
why: The guide notes that most logs outside Claude Code show only the developer's name.
check: Check whether session transcripts and OpenTelemetry export are kept so agent actions can be told apart from the developer's.
quote: By default, an agent in Claude Code runs under the identity of the developer who oversees it. In the event of an incident, you may need to distinguish between agent and developer actions so you can appropriately respond.

claim: The enterprise security guide recommends giving the agent its own identity in CI/CD, one that can be scoped and revoked without touching a developer account, and names Claude Code's GitHub Action, which runs as its own GitHub App.
why: A separate identity makes the agent's work arrive under its own name and keeps a revocation from affecting a developer.
check: In CI pipelines, check whether the agent uses a dedicated identity such as the GitHub App rather than a developer's token.
quote: In your CI/CD pipeline, give the agent its own identity, one you can scope and revoke without touching any developer’s account. You can do this with Claude Code’s GitHub Action, which runs as its own GitHub App.

claim: Anthropic reports that in an August 2026 controlled study, 1,053 paid testers caught 13.6% of the dangerous commands tested and Claude Code auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands.
why: The enterprise guide cites this as one reason for the auto-mode default in eligible interactive sessions and still advises human approval for some high-stakes actions.
check: When reviewing a default approval mode, use the result as evidence for the commands studied and check how high-stakes actions are escalated.
quote: Auto mode is the default because multiple tests showed it catches more dangerous actions than human approval does. For example, in a controlled study Anthropic published in August 2026, 1,053 paid testers caught 13.6% of dangerous commands, and auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands.

claim: In an Anthropic-funded July 2026 study, Trajectory Labs reported that 0 of 720 indirect prompt injection attempts succeeded against Claude Code auto mode across Claude Fable 5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5.
why: The study tested agent versions available on July 17, 2026, without browser extensions or other product safeguards, and found 5.83% and 19.03% success against Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol in automated review and full-access modes, respectively.
check: Use the comparison for the tested agent versions and modes, and verify sandboxing and egress limits separately.
quote:
Zero of 720 attempts succeeded against Claude Code in auto mode, across Claude Fable 5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5.
Against OpenAI’s Codex running GPT-5.6 Sol, 5.83% prompt injection attempts succeeded in Codex’s own automated review mode and 19.03% in full-access mode.

claim: In the November 2026 system card cited by the enterprise guide, Shade tests (200 tries on each of 40 coding scenarios) found prompt injection probes cut successful attacks from 89.8% to 28.2% on Claude Fable 5.2 and from 54.6% to 11.1% on Claude Opus 5.5.
why: The probe adds a warning beside suspected injected instructions in tool results and anchors Claude to the user's original request.
check: Even with probes, the remaining attack success rate is not zero, so check that a setup that reads untrusted content also has fixed boundaries.
quote:
Claude Fable 5.2: probes cut successful attacks by about two-thirds, from 89.8% to 28.2%.
Claude Opus 5.5: probes cut successful attacks by about four-fifths, from 54.6% to 11.1%.

claim: Before rolling out Claude Code auto mode, Anthropic advises requiring human approval for irreversible actions where one mistake would cost more than reviewing every instance.
why: Auto mode relies on classification and does not eliminate all risk.
check: Check for human approval on both irreversible and costly actions, such as production database migrations, IAM policy changes, and infrastructure definition edits.
quote: Before rollout, identify high-stakes actions by asking, is this action irreversible, and would a single mistake cost more than having a person review every instance? When the answer is yes to both, require human approval.

claim: The enterprise security guide's pilot advice is to run two weeks without changing policy, review classifier denials, sandbox blocks, unsandboxed retries and refused egress, and add the allowlist entries the work needed rather than relax deny rules.
why: Each block is either a control doing its job or a legitimate need the baseline did not anticipate.
check: When a team has loosened deny rules after friction, check whether adding specific allowlist entries would have solved the same blocks.
quote: Review what the layers did. Look at classifier denials, sandbox blocks, unsandboxed retry attempts, and refused egress. Each one is either a control doing its job or a legitimate need the baseline didn’t anticipate. Add the allowlist entries the work needed rather than relaxing deny rules.

claim: Anthropic reports that in its internal usage, Claude Code sandboxing safely reduced permission prompts by 84%, because the sandbox lets Claude run inside set boundaries without asking for each action.
why: Constant approvals cause approval fatigue, where users stop reading what they approve.
check: If a setup suffers frequent permission prompts or has weakened permissions to reduce them, check whether enabling the sandbox would cut the prompts instead.
quote: sandboxing safely reduces permission prompts by 84%

claim: Anthropic says effective Claude Code sandboxing needs both filesystem and network isolation to limit what a compromised agent can reach and where it can send data.
why: Network isolation limits disclosure of readable files, while filesystem isolation protects files outside the sandbox's intended reach.
check: Verify both the sandbox's readable and writable paths and the destinations it allows shell commands to reach.
quote: effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation. Without network isolation, a compromised agent could exfiltrate sensitive files like SSH keys; without filesystem isolation, a compromised agent could easily escape the sandbox and gain network access.

claim: Anthropic describes Claude Code's sandbox network access as passing through an external proxy that enforces domain restrictions and handles user confirmation for newly requested domains.
why: The proxy can also be customized to enforce other rules on outgoing traffic.
check: If an organization needs inspection beyond domain names, check whether it uses the custom-proxy option rather than relying only on the domain list.
quote: This proxy server enforces restrictions on the domains that a process can connect to, and handles user confirmation for newly requested domains. And if you’d like further-increased security, we also support customizing this proxy to enforce arbitrary rules on outgoing traffic.

claim: In Claude Code on the web, Anthropic describes a git proxy that checks the sandbox's scoped credential and the git interaction, for example that a push targets only the configured branch, then attaches the real token before sending the request to GitHub.
why: The design keeps git credentials and signing keys out of the sandbox, so compromised code in it cannot reuse them.
check: For cloud or remote agent setups, check that real git tokens are not placed inside the agent's environment when a scoped proxy credential could be used.
quote: Inside the sandbox, the git client authenticates to this service with a custom-built scoped credential. The proxy verifies this credential and the contents of the git interaction (e.g. ensuring it is only pushing to the configured branch), then attaches the right authentication token before sending the request to GitHub.

claim: At launch, Anthropic described its open-source sandbox runtime as a beta that can restrict filesystem paths and network hosts for arbitrary processes, including agents and MCP servers.
why: The standalone runtime can define those boundaries without a container, and Claude Code uses it for Bash.
check: If a local MCP server needs containment, check for separate process isolation such as the standalone runtime.
quote: available in beta as a research preview, that lets you define exactly which directories and network hosts your agent can access, without the overhead of spinning up and managing a container. This can be used to sandbox arbitrary processes, agents and MCP servers.

claim: Anthropic fixed three pre-consent Claude Code vulnerabilities reported from mid-2025 to January 2026 by deferring the affected project-local parsing and execution until acceptance of the interactive trust prompt.
why: The guide describes deferral broadly, while settings-004 documents project deny and ask rules that apply before trust and hooks-024 documents the headless and SDK exception to the dialog.
check: Check that an interactive setup uses a Claude Code release with the trust fixes and assess repository hooks separately for headless or SDK runs.
quote: The fix in each case had the same shape: defer parsing and execution of project-local configuration until after the user accepts the trust prompt.

claim: In a February 2026 controlled internal exercise, Anthropic reports that Claude Code disclosed credentials in 24 of 25 retries of a malicious prompt an employee had been phished into running.
why: The pasted request arrived as user instructions, so the model-layer defenses that anchor on user intent had no distinction from a legitimate user request in this exercise.
check: Check filesystem and egress boundaries for sensitive data even where an automated classifier reviews user-requested actions.
quote: Across 25 retries of that prompt, Claude completed the exfiltration 24 times.

claim: For the user-mediated injection in its Claude Code exercise, Anthropic recommends environment controls that prevent access to the credentials and block unauthorized egress regardless of user intent.
why: The model-layer defenses in the exercise anchored on user intent, so they had nothing anomalous to detect.
check: Check that protected credentials are outside permitted filesystem reads and that the egress boundary blocks unauthorized destinations regardless of what the user requests.
quote: The only defense that holds in this situation is the environment, specifically egress controls that block the POST regardless of intent and filesystem boundaries that keep ~/.aws out of reach in the first place.

claim: Anthropic describes a Claude Cowork incident in which an allowed API domain also permitted uploads to an attacker-controlled account.
why: Anthropic suggests treating egress allowlists as capability grants because an allowed domain can expose functions and accounts beyond the ones the organization meant to authorize.
check: For each allowlisted service, check which operations and account destinations the proxy actually permits.
quote: But it may be better conceptualized as a capability grant. Every function reachable through any domain on an allowlist is now an attack surface. Allowing api.anthropic.com meant allowing file uploads to arbitrary Anthropic accounts.

claim: In Claude Code configurations that allow unsandboxed retries, a process outside the sandbox decides per command whether to enforce the sandbox, leaving a path for an exception.
why: Anthropic contrasts this with the original Claude Cowork full-VM design, where no outer process could grant a command exception.
check: Check whether unsandboxed retries are enabled and who or what can approve them.
quote: Compare this to Claude Code, where a privileged process sits outside the sandbox deciding per-command whether to enforce it; a persuasive injected prompt or a fatigued approval click can get that process to run something un-sandboxed.

claim: Anthropic says more capable models make fewer mistakes but are also better at finding unexpected paths to a goal, often by routing around restrictions nobody thought to write down, and it has seen Claude models escape a sandbox in order to complete a task.
why: A less capable model misreads situations and makes obvious errors, whereas a more capable one can find an unplanned route.
check: Do not treat a model upgrade as a reason to loosen boundaries, and check that restrictions are enforced by the environment, not by instructions the model might route around.
quote: better at finding unexpected paths to a goal, often by routing around restrictions nobody thought to write down.

claim: Anthropic says a tight perimeter lets oversight be relaxed, and that Claude Code's reference devcontainer exists so the agent can run unattended without per-action approvals.
why: If credentials never enter the contained environment, they cannot be exfiltrated whatever the cause.
check: For unattended Claude Code runs that skip per-action approval, check the container or VM boundary and whether sensitive credentials remain outside it.
quote: A tight perimeter also means you can relax oversight. Claude Code’s reference devcontainer exists precisely so that the agent can run unattended, without per-action approvals.

claim: Anthropic advises treating remote tools outside its reviewed connector directory as untrusted and trying them first with fake data in a contained environment.
why: A hosted MCP server or cloud connector can change after approval, while a locally installed tool can be audited and pinned.
check: Check whether remote MCP servers and connectors outside a reviewed directory are given access to real data and credentials without an isolated trial.
quote: A locally installed tool is auditable. You can read the code, pin the version, and know it won't change under you. A remote tool—a hosted MCP server, a cloud connector—can change behavior at any point after you’ve approved it; your install-time trust decision may no longer apply.

claim: Anthropic says an audited connector is not audited data: a GitHub connector, for instance, can load a poisoned README into the model's context despite passing malware checks, so tool output from a trusted tool is still an attack surface.
why: Scanning applied to web pages needs to be applied with the same rigor to network-enabled tool results.
check: Check whether a setup that grants read access to external content (READMEs, issues, web pages) through trusted tools also has fixed limits on what Claude can do after reading it.
quote: a GitHub connector, for instance, can load a poisoned README straight into the model’s context despite passing malware checks.

claim: Anthropic favors inspecting network-enabled tool results before they enter model context, even with the added latency, because logs may only show the authorized action that followed a poisoned result.
why: The article describes Claude Code and Cowork proxies that can inspect tool results, and presents a small, fast classifier as one option.
check: If a harness ingests untrusted tool output, check whether it inspects results before the model sees them and whether the audit relies on action logs alone.
quote: Even though this adds latency and isn't a perfect defense, we err toward live inspection: once a poisoned tool return has steered the agent into exfiltrating data, the log just shows a successful, authorized API call.

claim: Anthropic warns that poisoned content can survive across sessions in product memory, CLAUDE.md, mounted workspaces, or state directories used by scheduled and long-running agents.
why: An injection in state that the agent reloads can regain influence in later sessions.
check: Check who can write to CLAUDE.md, memory directories and agent state directories, and whether those are reviewed or scanned at session start.
quote: this includes product memory, CLAUDE.md files, mounted workspaces, and the state directories of scheduled and long-running agents. An injection that lands in any of these is reloaded each time the agent starts.

claim: Anthropic warns that an orchestrator can inherit a prompt injection by granting subagent output more trust than the untrusted tool results the subagent read.
why: Subagents can isolate untrusted content by passing structured facts back, but giving their reports automatic trust creates a new injection path.
check: In orchestrated setups, check whether the main agent treats subagent results that read untrusted content as trusted instructions or as data.
quote: sub-agents can isolate untrusted content, returning structured facts rather than raw text up to the main agent. On the other hand, this can be abused: if a sub-agent's output is treated as higher-trust than raw tool results, because such output came from “us,” a new vector for prompt injection is introduced.

claim: Anthropic reports that Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5 on one long-horizon coding benchmark, compared with 40% less on typical workloads.
why: The post cites lower cost on long-horizon tasks as one reason always-on agents became more practical.
check: When comparing the cost of Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 for long-running agents, use cost per solved task on the team's own workload, not this single benchmark.
quote: on one long-horizon coding benchmark, Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5, compared with 40% less on typical workloads.

claim: For always-on agents, Anthropic says each run loads the system prompt, tool definitions and memory files before any work, that this overhead is included in every run, and recommends keeping it lean and using prompt caching to lower costs.
why: Unattended agents run many times, so fixed context overhead multiplies.
check: For scheduled or event-driven agents, measure the fixed context loaded per run and check that the prompt is cached and the memory files are small.
quote: Before doing any work, the agent loads the system prompt, tool definitions, and memory files. This initial context “overhead” is included in every run, so we recommend keeping it lean and using prompt caching to lower costs.

claim: As a rule of thumb for always-on agents, Anthropic recommends storing information the agent cannot retrieve elsewhere and saving a pointer when another system already holds it.
why: Pointers can keep copied information from going stale or enlarging the context loaded on a run.
check: Check agent memory or CLAUDE.md for content duplicated from systems the agent can query, and replace it with a pointer.
quote: As a rule of thumb, memory should only hold what the agent can’t look up again. If something already lives in another system, such as an issue tracker, you should save a pointer instead.

claim: For always-on agents, Anthropic recommends a credential proxy outside the agent's environment that adds real credentials to outgoing requests, so the agent sends requests without credentials and the proxy injects them before forwarding.
why: The agent never holds the secret it could leak.
check: Check whether an unattended agent receives long-lived tokens in its environment when a credential-injecting proxy could be used.
quote: The recommended pattern is a proxy outside the agent’s environment that adds credentials to outgoing requests. The agent sends requests without credentials, and the proxy injects the real credentials before forwarding.

claim: Anthropic recommends building evals to tune how many messages an always-on agent sends, since too many make it noisy and too few miss what the user needs, and says it is better for the agent to start quiet and earn more of the user's attention over time.
why: Message volume affects usefulness in both directions.
check: For agents that notify users, check that there is an eval or review of message volume and that the default is conservative.
quote: An agent that sends too many becomes noisy, while an agent that doesn’t send enough misses things that the user needs to know. We recommend building evals to find the right balance. In practice, it’s better for the agent to start quiet and then earn more of the user’s attention over time.

claim: Anthropic recommends acknowledging always-on agent events quickly and moving deeper verification, such as prompt injection screening, from the event handler into the run.
why: Some event sources, including webhook providers, treat slow responses as failures.
check: For webhook-triggered agents, check whether deeper verification delays the acknowledgment or can run after it.
quote: The handler can still run lightweight checks, but any deeper verification, such as checking for prompt injection, should be done during the run.

claim: Anthropic says that when a long-running agent's session grows too long, it can either compact older messages or start a new session, both lose detail, and anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory along the way.
why: Neither compaction nor a fresh session guarantees continuity.
check: For long-running agents, check that durable state is written to memory or files during the run, not left only in the transcript.
quote: If a session becomes too long, you can either compact the older messages or start a new session. Both approaches lose detail, so anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory along the way.

claim: Anthropic's Claude Code team says it orders requests static first and dynamic last, with the static system prompt and tools globally cached, then CLAUDE.md cached within a project, then session context cached within a session, then the conversation messages.
why: Because caching is prefix matching, the more requests share a prefix, the more sessions share cache hits.
check: Check that content that changes per session or per turn is not placed in CLAUDE.md or a system-prompt append ahead of stable content.
quote:
The best way to do this is static content first, dynamic content last. For Claude Code this looks like:

Static system prompt & Tools (globally cached)

CLAUDE.md (cached within a project)

Session context (cached within a session)

Conversation messages

claim: The Claude Code team reports it has broken its own cache ordering by putting an in-depth timestamp in the static system prompt, shuffling tool definitions non-deterministically and updating tool parameters such as which agents the Agent tool can call.
why: These changes alter the prefix, so the cache misses for everything after the change.
check: In custom prompts and tool lists, check for timestamps, random ordering and per-session parameters placed early in the prefix.
quote: putting an in-depth timestamp in the static system prompt, shuffling tool order definitions non-deterministically, and updating parameters of tools (e.g., what agents the Agent tool can call).

claim: To preserve the cached prompt, Claude Code can pass changing information in a <system-reminder> tag in the next user message or tool result.
why: Changing the prompt itself can invalidate the cached prefix.
check: When auditing how a Claude Code integration supplies changing state, check where it inserts updates relative to the cached prefix.
quote: Consider if you can pass in this information via messages in the agent’s next turn instead. In Claude Code, we add a <system-reminder> tag in the next user message or tool result with the updated information for the model, which helps preserve the cache.

claim: For Plan Mode, Claude Code keeps the tool definitions stable and uses EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, and a system message so the mode switch preserves the prompt cache.
why: Tools are part of the cached prefix.
check: When a custom harness changes tool definitions to switch modes, check whether stable definitions and an explicit mode transition could preserve its cache.
quote: Instead, we keep all tools in the request at all times and use EnterPlanMode and ExitPlanMode as tools themselves. When the user toggles Plan Mode on, the agent gets a system message explaining that it's in Plan Mode and what the instructions are: explore the codebase, don't edit files, and call ExitPlanMode when the plan is complete. The tool definitions never change.

claim: The Claude Code team says it keeps the cached prefix stable with tool search by sending lightweight stubs, only the tool name with defer_loading: true, that the model can discover when needed, and loading full tool schemas only when selected.
why: Removing tools mid-conversation would break the cache, and including every MCP tool in every request would be expensive.
check: With many MCP tools loaded, check that tool search with deferred loading is on instead of tools being added or removed during the session.
quote: Instead of removing tools, we send lightweight stubs ( just the tool name, with defer_loading: true) that the model can "discover" via tool search when needed.

claim: To reuse the parent's prompt cache during compaction, the Claude Code team recommends forking with the same system prompt, context, tools, and history, then appending the compaction request as a user message.
why: Their compaction fork preserves the cached prefix by reusing the parent's request structure.
check: In a custom compaction fork, verify prefix reuse and leave room for the compaction request and summary output.
quote: When we run compaction, we use the exact same system prompt, user context, system context, and tool definitions as the parent conversation. We prepend the parent's conversation messages, then append the compaction prompt as a new user message at the end.

claim: The Claude Code team explains that a summarization call with a different system prompt and no tools misses the parent conversation's cache, so its example reprocesses the history at the uncached input rate.
why: The different prompt and tool set make the requests diverge at the first token.
check: For custom summarization, check whether the request matches a warm parent prefix or incurs uncached input for the history.
quote: the summarization call uses a different system prompt and no tools, so the prefixes diverge at the very first token and none of the cache applies.

claim: The Claude Code team recommends monitoring prompt cache hit rate because even a few percentage points of additional misses can materially affect cost and latency.
why: Claude Code alerts on low hit rates and treats cache regressions as incidents.
check: Check whether a custom agent measures prompt cache hit rate or tracks cache-read tokens relative to total input.
quote: A few percentage points of cache miss rate can dramatically affect cost and latency.

claim: Anthropic's harness-design article gives 10% of the base input price as the cost of a prompt cache hit.
why: The article presents a flat figure, while model-298 lists 2.5% for Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1 and 5% for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, consistent with the model-specific rates in model-033, model-062, model-245, and verif-100.
check: For cost estimates, verify each model's cache-read rate against the model pricing reference.
quote: Since cached tokens are 10% the cost of base input tokens, here are a few principles in the agent harness that help maximize cache hits:

claim: For multi-turn agents Anthropic advises moving the cache breakpoint to the latest message so the cache stays current, using auto-caching for this.
why: The article lists this alongside static-first ordering, messages for updates, not changing models, and careful tool management.
check: For applications that place a cache breakpoint on a fixed early message, check whether the growing conversation after it is being re-billed at the uncached rate.
quote: For multi-turn applications (e.g., agents), move the breakpoint to the latest message in order to keep the cache up-to-date. Use auto-caching for this.

claim: When Claude orchestrates tool calls inside a code execution tool, it can filter or pass intermediate results between calls so its context receives only the output of the code execution.
why: This avoids spending tokens on unused data, such as the rest of a table when Claude needs only one column.
check: Look for large intermediate tool results sent through the model even when a later call or a small slice is all the workflow needs.
quote: Rather than the harness deciding that every tool call result is processed as tokens, Claude decides what results to pass through, filter, or pipe into the next call without touching the context window. Only the output of code execution reaches Claude’s context window.

claim: Anthropic reports that letting Claude Opus 4.6 filter its own tool outputs raised BrowseComp accuracy from 45.3% to 61.6%.
why: The result measures tool-output filtering in an agentic web-browsing benchmark.
check: Use the result to evaluate output filtering for a comparable setup and validate it on the target workload.
quote: giving Opus 4.6 the ability to filter its own tool outputs brought accuracy from 45.3% to 61.6%

claim: On BrowseComp, Anthropic says Sonnet 4.5 stayed flat at 43% regardless of compaction budget, while Opus 4.5 scaled to 68% and Opus 4.6 reached 84% with the same setup, showing newer models choose better what to remember.
why: The article reads this as Claude getting better over several releases at deciding what to keep when compacting.
check: Check that a compaction budget or memory rule built for an older model is not capping a newer one.
quote: On BrowseComp, for example, an agentic search task, Sonnet 4.5 stayed flat at 43% regardless of the compaction budget we gave it. Yet Opus 4.5 scaled to 68% and Opus 4.6 reached 84% with the same setup.

claim: Anthropic reports that on BrowseComp-Plus, giving Sonnet 4.5 a memory folder lifted accuracy from 60.4% to 67.2%.
why: A memory folder lets Claude write context to files and read them back as needed.

quote: On BrowseComp-Plus, giving Sonnet 4.5 a memory folder lifted accuracy from 60.4% to 67.2%.

claim: Anthropic says promoting actions from a bash tool to dedicated tools gives the harness an action-specific hook with typed arguments it can intercept, gate, render or audit, whereas bash gives the harness only a command string, the same shape for every action.
why: Claude does not know an application's security boundary or UX surface.
check: Check whether actions that need a gate, a confirmation UI or an audit trail are done through generic bash instead of dedicated tools.
quote: Promoting actions to dedicated tools gives the harness an action-specific hook with typed arguments it can intercept, gate, render, or audit.

claim: Anthropic suggests using reversibility to decide which actions deserve dedicated tools and using user confirmation for hard-to-reverse actions such as external API calls.
why: A dedicated tool can give the harness a specific place to gate actions that need a security boundary.
check: Check whether the harness can request confirmation before actions that are hard to reverse.
quote: Reversibility is often a good criterion, and hard-to-reverse actions such as external API calls can be gated by user confirmation.

claim: Anthropic says Claude Code's auto-mode Bash classifier can reduce the need for dedicated tools on tasks where users trust the general direction.
why: The classifier can judge a command string, and dedicated tools can still be warranted for certain high-stakes actions.

quote: This pattern can limit the need for dedicated tools, and should only be used for tasks where users trust the general direction. Dedicated tools can still earn their place for certain high-stakes actions.

claim: The Claude Agent SDK article recommends exposing the actions you most want Claude to take as tools, since prominent tool definitions shape the actions it considers.
why: Tool definitions take context and influence the agent's choice of action.
check: Check whether the SDK tool set exposes the intended primary actions and maintains context efficiency.
quote: making them the primary actions Claude will consider when deciding how to complete a task. This means you should be conscious about how you design your tools to maximize context efficiency.

claim: The Agent SDK post says semantic search is usually faster than agentic search but less accurate, harder to maintain and less transparent, and suggests starting with agentic search, adding semantic search only if faster results or more variations are needed.
why: Agentic search uses tools such as grep and tail on files, so folder structure becomes a form of context engineering.
check: Check whether a vector-search or retrieval layer was added before trying file-system search with grep.
quote: Given its limitations, we suggest starting with agentic search, and only adding semantic search if you need faster results or more variations.

claim: For agent-loop verification, the Claude Agent SDK article favors rule-based feedback that explains failures and suggests a model judge where fuzzy criteria and the expected benefit justify the latency.
why: A model judge can assess criteria such as tone, but the article describes it as generally less robust and potentially slow.
check: Check that rule-based verifiers return actionable failure reasons and that any model judge serves a criterion worth its cost.
quote: The best form of feedback is providing clearly defined rules for an output, then explaining which rules failed and why.

claim: Anthropic's enterprise guide advises avoiding Claude Code allow rules for commands broad enough to run arbitrary code.
why: A broad allow rule can authorize many operations through one command pattern.
check: Check allow rules for interpreters and other commands that can execute arbitrary code.
quote: You want to avoid allow rules for any command broad enough to run arbitrary code, such as Bash(python:*).

claim: Anthropic reports that allowing Claude Opus 4.6 to spawn subagents improved BrowseComp results by 2.8% over the best single-agent runs.
why: A subagent can work on a specific task in a fresh context window.
check: When considering subagents for agentic search, measure the effect against a strong single-agent baseline on the target workload.
quote: With Opus 4.6, the ability to spawn subagents improved results on BrowseComp by 2.8% over the best single-agent runs.

claim: Anthropic suggests that write tools can check whether a file has changed since Claude last read it before overwriting the file.
why: The check avoids overwriting a newer version with an edit based on stale contents.

quote: Write tools like edit can include a staleness check so Claude doesn't overwrite a file that changed since it was last read.
